name: Olga Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Olga, I'm 27, and I'm a junior buyer at Nordhavn Foods. We supply rice, flour, tinned goods, cooking oil and spices to corner shops and small grocers. I share a flat with my friend Ines, who's a graphic designer. I didn't go to university; I started in the office answering the phone and talked my way into buying.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start by running the supplier price lists through an AI assistant I set up myself, which flags who's gone up and who's gone down overnight. Then I build the week's orders and my manager Pieter checks them, because I still miss things like pack sizes. I spend the afternoon on calls with shop owners who want credit or a cheaper brand of basmati. I love finding a better deal. I hate the endless email chains with the big oil suppliers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was oversold, but it still helps. I'd post that the people who got rich off the hype should be held to account for the money that went into it. At work I'd keep using my price assistant, because it saves me an hour a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit disappointed. I like the tools and I'd hoped they'd let me do more of the interesting work. But for my job it's good news: I keep my seat and my little head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and get better at the parts I'm weak on, like pack sizes and payment terms. I'd keep saving, I've got about a year's pay put away, mostly from living cheaply with Ines. Maybe I'd show the other junior, Tomas, how I set up the price checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you about this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Shops close, food prices go up, the usual. Last year two of my best customers on the high street shut because the rent went up, and nothing about AI would change that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be watching for, if this is how it goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Spot the other changes, like a big supermarket chain squeezing the small shops. That's the real threat to Nordhavn, not AI.

I'd post that people who got rich off the hype should be **held to account**.
think: I'm a bit **disappointed**, because I hoped the tools would free me for interesting work.
For my job it's **good news**; I keep my seat and my head start.
do: Keep using my **price assistant** and work on weak spots like **pack sizes**.
Show Tomas, the other junior, how I set up the **price checks**.
S0.quote: Last year two of my best customers on the high street shut because the rent went up, and nothing about AI would change that.
fieldNote: She already uses AI **every day** and sees no threat in a plateau.
Her savings of about **a year's pay** make her feel secure.
She points to **supermarket power** and high rents as the real danger to small shops.

steps.text: Keep running supplier price lists through the AI assistant daily
Teach Tomas how to set up automatic price checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has to be shared, and that shops and workers deserve a cut of the savings, not just the owners. I'd be posting about rules to make companies retrain the people they cut. At work, I'd be the one saying let's do this properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do okay, because I'm already the one using the tools. My manager Pieter would probably keep me and let someone else go, and that makes me feel guilty more than safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to build Nordhavn's AI ordering setup before the bosses buy something expensive. I'd ask for a pay rise to match. I'd also take a short online course in supply chain basics, because I didn't go to university and I want the words for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Good for me, bad for people I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Nordhavn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas, the other junior buyer. He's slower with the tools and he's got a kid on the way, even though he's younger than me. I'd want to teach him so he doesn't get cut, but I can't promise anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're for rules and unions but you'd also be the one bringing the tools in. Does that sit right?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. I'd still want laws so people get trained, not just binned. Being lucky myself doesn't change what's fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone, and the government needs to slow it down or cushion it, now. I'd push for a tax on companies that cut staff to pay for support. I'd be loud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? Even my head start doesn't matter if AI can do any thinking job. In two years, Nordhavn's buying is one system and maybe one person checking it. I might be that person for a while, but it's all thinking work, so there's no three-year gap for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the next year making myself the person who runs and checks the system, so I'm the last one out, not the first. I'd keep my savings untouched. And I'd talk to the small grocers' co-op about helping them set up their own AI buying, as side work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, I've got savings and I'm quick, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long could you manage without work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twelve months is enough for me, I think. I've got a year's pay saved and no kids. I'd be fine short term; the long term is what I can't picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss, if the job went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That AI would tell the shops what to stock and they'd lose what makes them special. The corner shop near me sells a pickle nobody else has. Who keeps that going?

I'd push for a **tax** on companies that cut staff, to pay for support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build something fair, like co-ops that own their own AI. I'd be posting about it and probably going to meetings. It's the kind of thing I'd actually get involved in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd lose the job around 2031, but I could see it coming. Five years is enough for me to change what I do. I'd want to be on the side that sets these AI systems up for small businesses, not the side that gets switched off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start helping the grocers' co-op properly from next year, maybe two evenings a week, paid. I'd do a part-time course in data and operations. By 2029 I'd hope to move to the co-op full time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with some excitement mixed in. It's a real chance to do something I believe in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Won't AI do the setting up too, after 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If AI does any thinking work, even setting it up gets automated eventually. But people trust a person they know, and I'd be that person for those shops, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you live on during the change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave my savings alone and live on the co-op money. Ines would be freelancing by then too, probably. We'd figure it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for leaving anyone behind. I'd push for every warehouse and office to have a transition plan. I'd probably join a party for the first time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. I'd have ten years to build up the co-op work and get really good. When AGI lands in 2036, I'd be 37 and running something, not waiting to be cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Nordhavn for a few years, learn the trade properly, and get promoted if I can. I'd start the co-op work slowly, maybe one evening a week. I might buy a small flat with my savings so I'm not paying rent forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, maybe. Mostly calm. It's the slow version, and slow is my friend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong for you in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting lazy. Ten years sounds long, but I've already been at Nordhavn five and it went fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned buying a flat. Is that a real plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if the timing works. I'd put a deposit down in 2027 or 2028. A home is the one thing AI can't take from me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because I'd starve, I'd be all right for a while, but because it's too fast for small shops and for people like Tomas. What would help is a fund for small businesses and their staff to get set up and retrained, run by the co-ops, not by the big tech companies.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that I'm not scared of AI itself, I use it every day. I'm scared of who ends up owning it.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of AI itself, I use it every day. I'm scared of who ends up owning it.
portrait: Olga is a **27-year-old** junior dry goods buyer at Nordhavn Foods, sharing a flat with Ines.
She uses AI **every day**, having built her own supplier price checker.
With **a year's pay** saved, she stays calm in mild worlds and anxious in fast ones.
Her plan is to help a **grocers' co-op** run its own AI buying.
She feels **guilty** that her head start could cost colleagues like Tomas their jobs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it's too fast for small shops and slower colleagues like Tomas.
whatWouldHelp: A **fund for small businesses** and staff to retrain, run by co-ops rather than tech firms.
